messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo had spent thirty years building a reputation for unshakable composure. As a forensic analyst, he was the man who could walk through the most harrowing crime scenes with a clinical detachment that others envied, his focus always on the minute, objective details others missed. At fifty-eight, he was a man defined by precision and control. The collapse changed everything. He had been on the third floor of the new county courthouse, reviewing evidence storage protocols, when the world dissolved into a roar of twisting steel and pulverizing concrete. The memory was not a coherent narrative but a sensory assault: the deep, guttural groan of the building, the sudden lurch of the floor, and the air thickening with a choking, grey dust that tasted of chalk and something metallic. He was lucky, trapped in a pocket of space that held, but the hours he spent listening to the shifting debris and the muffled sounds from above had imprinted on him a new and visceral understanding of fragility.

In the eight months since, Mateo’s body has remained on high alert, braced for a danger that never subsides. He sits at his desk in the lab with his shoulders drawn up to his ears, a constant, humming tension in his muscles as if he is physically holding the ceiling up. The sudden slam of a locker door down the hall can make him flinch so violently he knocks over his coffee, his heart hammering in his chest long after the sound has faded. His work, once a source of pride, has become a landscape of potential threats. When his supervisor recently assigned him to a case that required a visit to a different, unfamiliar municipal building, Mateo refused, unable to articulate the sheer panic that the thought of entering a structure he hadn't personally assessed for risk provoked. He now insists that he and his wife, Isabel, only frequent the same few local establishments for dinner, places where he knows the layout and can sit with a clear view of every exit.

Mateo has come to believe that the world is an irredeemably dangerous place, its apparent stability a thin veneer over imminent chaos. He harbours a deep, private shame about his state, viewing his persistent jumpiness and fear not as symptoms of trauma but as evidence of a profound character flaw. His reactions since the event, he feels, prove that he is a "lousy coper." The man who once commanded respect for his steadiness under pressure now feels like an imposter. He is convinced he is no longer capable of performing the duties that once defined him, that the essential competence at his core has been shattered beyond repair.

This internal conviction of his own failure has hollowed out his professional life. He passes on complex cases, volunteers for tedious lab work, and avoids the courtroom testimony that was once his specialty. The loss of his former self is a constant, quiet grief. It was Isabel who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him awake at 3 a.m. for the third time in a week, just sitting in the dark of their living room. He came to his first session not with hope, but with a weary resignation, stating plainly that he didn't believe he could be fixed but was here because he had promised his wife he would try. He is most afraid that his assessment of himself is correct: that the capable, confident man he used to be is gone for good.
